title: Statistical inference | Deep learning refresher
objectives: Explain p-values, power and confidence intervals precisely. Rebuild backprop intuition before transformers.
exercise: Write a power calculator: given baseline conversion, MDE, α and power, return n per arm, then verify it by simulation. Separately, follow Karpathy's micrograd lecture and train a tiny MLP.
resources: Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Ch. 1 free at experimentguide.com)
Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero (micrograd, makemore)
fast.ai Practical Deep Learning for Coders

cards.q: True or false: p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
cards.explain: The p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data).

cards.q: The p-value is…
choices: The probability, assuming H0 is true, of a result at least as extreme as observed
The probability the result will replicate
The effect size divided by its standard error

cards.q: Correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval [1.2%, 3.4%]?
choices: The procedure that produced it covers the true effect in 95% of repeated experiments
There is a 95% probability the true effect is in [1.2%, 3.4%]
95% of users had an effect in that range
The effect is 95% likely to be positive
cards.explain: In frequentist terms, once computed the interval either contains the parameter or it doesn't. The 95% describes the procedure.

cards.q: A test returns p = 0.25. What can you conclude?
choices: We failed to reject H0; the data are compatible with no effect, but the test may be underpowered
H0 is 75% likely to be true
cards.explain: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Check power and the CI width.

cards.q: A two-sided z-test gives z = 2.5. What is the p-value? (decimal, 3 dp)
If you halve the MDE, by what factor does the required sample size change?
cards.explain: n ∝ 1/δ². Halving δ multiplies n by 4.

cards.q: Sample size per arm for a two-sample test of means (equal variance σ², difference δ)?
cards.explain: With α=0.05 and 80% power, (1.96 + 0.84)² ≈ 7.85, giving the rule of thumb n ≈ 16σ²/δ².

cards.q: Baseline conversion 10%, absolute MDE 1 percentage point, α = 0.05 two-sided, 80% power. Approximate n per arm?
cards.explain: Using σ² = p(1−p) = 0.09: n = 2·0.09·7.85/0.01² ≈ 14,100. Using p₁(1−p₁)+p₂(1−p₂) gives ≈14,800. Both are acceptable.

cards.q: Statistical power is…
choices: P(reject H0 | the effect equals the MDE): 1 − β
The size of the treatment effect

cards.q: Which of these does NOT increase power?
cards.explain: A stricter α makes rejection harder, which reduces power.

cards.q: What z-value corresponds to 80% power, i.e. z₁₋β for β = 0.2? (2 dp)
You test 20 metrics at α = 0.05 with no true effects. Expected number of false positives?
cards.explain: 20 × 0.05 = 1, by linearity of expectation.

cards.q: Same 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, all nulls true. P(at least one false positive)? Answer in %.
Bonferroni per-test threshold for 20 tests at family-wise α = 0.05?
Bonferroni controls ___, Benjamini–Hochberg controls ___.
choices: Type II error; Type I error
cards.explain: FWER = P(any false positive). FDR = expected share of rejections that are false.

cards.q: Order the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (m tests, FDR level q).
items: Find the largest k with p(k) ≤ (k/m)·q
Report the discoveries with FDR ≤ q

cards.q: Why does a ratio metric like clicks/sessions need the delta method or bootstrap when users are the randomisation unit?
cards.answer: Sessions from the same user are correlated, and both numerator and denominator are random sums over users. Treating sessions as i.i.d. understates the variance, which inflates false positives. The delta method (or a user-level bootstrap) gives the variance of a ratio of user-level means, including the numerator–denominator covariance.
rubric: Analysis unit (session) ≠ randomisation unit (user) means non-i.i.d.
Naive SE too small → false positives

cards.q: A nonparametric bootstrap sample is drawn by…
choices: Resampling n observations with replacement from the data
cards.explain: Permuting labels is a permutation test, which is a different tool.

cards.q: Users are randomised, and the metric is per-session CTR. What should the bootstrap resample?
cards.explain: Resample the independent unit, which is the randomisation unit.

cards.q: The delta method approximates the variance of g(X̄) by…
choices: A first-order Taylor expansion: Var ≈ g'(μ)² Var(X̄) (gradient form for multivariate)

cards.q: In the delta-method variance of a ratio X̄/Ȳ, which term is easy to forget?
choices: The covariance between numerator and denominator
cards.explain: Var(X̄/Ȳ) ≈ (1/μᵧ²)[Var(X̄) − 2(μₓ/μᵧ)Cov(X̄,Ȳ) + (μₓ/μᵧ)²Var(Ȳ)].

cards.q: For f = (a·b) + c, what is ∂f/∂a?
f = (a·b) + c with a = 2, b = −3, c = 10. What is ∂f/∂b?
A node's output feeds two downstream branches. Its gradient is…
choices: The sum of the gradients flowing back from both branches
Taken from the first branch only
cards.explain: Multivariate chain rule. This is why micrograd uses += for .grad.

cards.q: Derivative of the sigmoid σ(x) at x = 0?
Why do deep sigmoid networks suffer vanishing gradients?
choices: σ' ≤ 0.25, and saturated units have σ' ≈ 0; products of many such terms shrink toward 0
cards.explain: ReLU, residual connections and normalisation mitigate it.

cards.q: What two moving averages does Adam maintain?
choices: The gradient (1st moment) and the squared gradient (2nd moment)

cards.q: Why does Adam apply bias correction?
choices: The moving averages start at zero and are biased toward zero in early steps

cards.q: SGD with momentum…
choices: Uses an exponentially weighted average of past gradients, damping oscillation

cards.q: Training loss explodes to NaN after a few hundred steps. Most likely first fix?
choices: Lower the learning rate (and/or add warmup / gradient clipping)

cards.q: How does AdamW differ from Adam with L2 regularisation?
choices: Weight decay is decoupled from the adaptive gradient update

cards.q: Why does LayerNorm suit transformers better than BatchNorm?
cards.answer: LayerNorm normalises each token's features independently, so it doesn't depend on batch statistics. It works the same with batch size 1 at inference, with variable sequence lengths and padding, and with autoregressive decoding. BatchNorm's batch statistics are noisy for small batches and awkward across padded sequences.
rubric: LN normalises per example/token across features
Independent of batch size; same at train and inference

cards.q: Why not initialise all weights to zero?
choices: Symmetry: every neuron in a layer gets identical gradients and never differentiates

cards.q: He (Kaiming) initialisation for ReLU layers uses weight variance…
cards.explain: ReLU zeroes half the inputs, hence the factor 2. Xavier uses 2/(fan_in + fan_out) for tanh.

cards.q: At inference, BatchNorm normalises using…
With 'inverted dropout' (p = 0.1), what happens at inference?
choices: Dropout is off; no rescaling is needed because training already scaled by 1/(1−p)

cards.q: What does loss.backward() populate, and why do you call optimizer.zero_grad()?
cards.answer: It fills .grad on every leaf tensor with requires_grad=True (the parameters) with ∂loss/∂param. PyTorch accumulates gradients (+=) by default, so you must zero them each step or they sum across iterations.

cards.q: Order one PyTorch training step.
cards.explain: zero_grad() only has to run before backward(); putting it first is the common convention.

cards.q: What does wrapping inference in torch.no_grad() do?
choices: Stops autograd recording the graph, saving memory and compute

cards.q: What does model.eval() change?
choices: Layer behaviour (dropout off, BatchNorm uses running stats); it does NOT disable gradients

cards.q: Setting requires_grad=True on a tensor means…
choices: Autograd records operations on it so gradients w.r.t. it can be computed
It will be updated by the optimizer automatically
cards.explain: The optimizer only updates the parameters you pass to it.
